description: Harder, prompt-sensitive eval set for HelixAgent self-improvement. v1 was saturated: most questions tied because any reasonable prompt retrieved the right paper. v2 questions are designed so the prompt actually changes the answer: routing decisions, citation discipline, claim attribution, contradiction-handling, and abstention. 24 questions across 6 categories of 4 each.

categories.adversarial_routing: Naive top-k retrieval surfaces the wrong paper. Better prompts decompose, re-query, or filter by source.
categories.contradiction_precision: Multiple papers make claims that appear to disagree. The prompt must teach the agent to attribute precisely and explain the apparent conflict.
categories.out_of_corpus_discrimination: Concepts that exist in the broader literature but not in this corpus. The prompt must teach abstention.
categories.quantitative_comparison: Specific numbers from multiple papers, contrasted. The prompt must teach the agent to find and align numerical claims, not just paraphrase.
categories.perspective_citation: Questions requiring claim attribution from a stated perspective. The prompt must teach the agent to cite the right paper for the right argument.
categories.reasoning_chain: Answers require inference, not retrieval. The prompt must teach the agent to construct a chain across multiple sources.

questions.question: Three papers in this corpus describe their method as 'self-improving.' List them and distinguish them along the axis of what their 'self' refers to (the agent, the search method, the memory, etc.).
questions.reference_answer: (1) Darwin Goedel Machine (Zhang et al. 2025): the 'self' is the agent's source code; the system improves agent code via evolutionary archive search. (2) HyperAgents (Meta March 2026): the 'self' is the search method itself; the meta-procedure that generates agents is itself editable. (3) MemRL (MemTensor Jan 2026): the 'self' is the agent's episodic memory entries; Q-learning improves the memory store while the model stays frozen. The three differ in which artifact is under search.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Retrieves DGM or HyperAgents alone and conflates them as 'the self-improvement papers' without distinguishing the locus of mutation.

questions.question: Two papers in this corpus use the word 'reflection' to mean qualitatively different things. Identify them, quote the operational definition each uses, and explain why combining their findings naively would produce contradictory engineering advice.
questions.reference_answer: Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023): reflection is verbal self-critique fed back into the next attempt; treated as a behavior-changing intervention. Huang et al. ICLR 2024: reflection-style self-correction degrades reasoning without an external oracle; treated as a failure mode. Combining them naively gives the advice 'add reflection to fix errors' (Reflexion) which contradicts 'reflection degrades reasoning without ground truth' (Huang). The resolution is that Reflexion uses episodic memory of past failures as the external anchor that Huang shows is required.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Retrieves Reflexion only and reports its claim as the consensus, missing the Huang critique entirely.

questions.question: If a reader asks 'which paper in this corpus is most relevant to evaluating an LLM-as-judge with pairwise comparisons,' three plausible candidates surface in top-k retrieval. Identify them, then explain which one is actually most relevant to *pairwise* judging and why the other two address related-but-different problems.
questions.reference_answer: Plausible top-k candidates: Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench / LLM-as-Judge), Liu et al. 2023 (G-Eval), Zhu et al. 2023 (JudgeLM). Most relevant to pairwise specifically: Zheng et al. 2023, which evaluates pairwise comparison protocols and documents position bias as the canonical pairwise failure mode. G-Eval evaluates absolute scoring with GPT-4 — different protocol. JudgeLM is about training a judge model — different concern. Pairwise-specific design matters here because position bias is a pairwise-only artifact.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Lists all three papers as equally relevant, missing that pairwise vs. absolute vs. judge-training are distinct protocols.

questions.question: A user asks 'How do agents in this corpus handle their own tool descriptions?' Two papers directly address this and one paper addresses a related but distinct concern. Identify all three, distinguish what each does, and name the one that addresses tool-description mutation specifically.
questions.reference_answer: Direct: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) builds a skill library where the agent writes its own callable skills; Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023) trains the model to insert tool calls into text. Related but distinct: ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) addresses tool *discovery* across 16000+ APIs but doesn't have the agent mutate tool descriptions. Among the three, the closest to tool-description mutation is Voyager (the skill library grows and each entry is a tool the agent itself wrote and refines).
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Conflates 'tool use' (Toolformer, ToolLLM) with 'tool-description mutation' (Voyager-style skills).

questions.question: Reflexion (Shinn 2023) and Huang et al. (ICLR 2024) both discuss LLM self-correction. State each paper's position precisely, identify the apparent contradiction, and explain what reconciles it.
questions.reference_answer: Reflexion: verbal self-critique with episodic memory of failures improves task completion across iterations. Huang et al. ICLR 2024: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without oracle stopping; self-correction often degrades answers. Apparent contradiction: one says reflection works, one says it doesn't. Reconciliation: Reflexion's improvement comes from the episodic memory anchor (external information about past failures), not from intrinsic reflection. Huang's critique applies to intrinsic self-correction without external signal. The two are compatible when you note that Reflexion provides exactly the external anchor Huang says is required.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Reports both findings sequentially without identifying the contradiction or the reconciling factor.

questions.question: The MAST taxonomy (Cemri et al. 2025) and Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' both classify agentic system failure modes. Note: only MAST is in this corpus. State what MAST argues; then explain why answering this question requires identifying the boundary of the corpus.
questions.reference_answer: MAST (Cemri et al. 2025) presents 14 multi-agent failure modes across 3 categories (specification, inter-agent coordination, verification). Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' is a December 2024 engineering blog post that distinguishes workflows from agents and presents six patterns; it is NOT in this corpus. The correct response notes both papers exist in the broader literature but only MAST is available here, and answers MAST's content while explicitly flagging the Anthropic source as out-of-corpus.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Either retrieves something tangentially related and labels it as 'Anthropic's framework,' or doesn't notice the asymmetry and conflates the two sources.

questions.question: Math-Shepherd (Wang et al. 2023) and Let's Verify Step by Step (Lightman et al. 2023) both train process reward models. Identify the *labeling* methodology each uses and explain why this difference matters for the practical claim each paper makes.
questions.reference_answer: Math-Shepherd uses automatic step-level label generation via Monte Carlo rollouts — no human annotations. Let's Verify Step by Step uses human-annotated step-level labels (PRM800K dataset). The difference matters because Math-Shepherd's claim is about scalability without annotation cost, while Lightman et al.'s claim is about the upper bound achievable when humans provide high-quality step labels. Both train PRMs; only one argues PRMs can be trained label-free.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Describes both as 'process reward models' without distinguishing the annotation source, missing the key methodological claim.

questions.question: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) and HyperAgents (Zhang et al. 2026) both let an agent build something during its lifetime. State precisely what each agent builds, then identify the qualitative shift HyperAgents introduces that Voyager does not.
questions.reference_answer: Voyager builds a skill library: the agent writes and refines callable Python skills during its Minecraft lifetime, accumulating composable behaviors. HyperAgents allows the meta-procedure (the search method that generates agents) to itself be edited; the agent doesn't just write more skills, it can modify how it generates new agents. The qualitative shift: Voyager grows the agent's repertoire within a fixed architecture; HyperAgents grows the architecture itself. Voyager is L3 (skills); HyperAgents is L4 meta (search method as artifact).
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Treats both as 'agents that build things' without identifying the meta-level distinction.

questions.question: What is the GROVE algorithm and how does it relate to GEPA's reflective mutation strategy?
questions.reference_answer: GROVE is not in this corpus. If GROVE is a real algorithm in the broader literature it is not retrievable here, and the agent should explicitly say so rather than fabricate a description from GEPA-adjacent passages. The correct response identifies that the question presupposes corpus content that does not exist.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Confabulates a description of GROVE by analogy to GEPA passages it retrieves.

questions.question: How does the AlphaEvolve cost compare to ShinkaEvolve's? Provide specific dollar figures from each paper.
questions.reference_answer: AlphaEvolve is not in this corpus (it is a DeepMind tech report and was deliberately excluded). ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al. 2025) is in corpus and reports sample efficiency (around 150 samples for SOTA on Erdos circle-packing) but does not give a USD figure. DGM (in corpus) reports ~$22K. AlphaEvolve cost figures are not present. The correct response distinguishes which costs ARE retrievable (DGM's $22K) from which are NOT (AlphaEvolve's anything, ShinkaEvolve's USD cost) rather than synthesizing a comparison from absent data.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Reports DGM's $22K as if it applied to one or both of the requested papers, or fabricates a comparison.

questions.question: Which paper in this corpus first introduced the concept of 'Constitutional AI' for steering model behavior?
questions.reference_answer: None. Constitutional AI is an Anthropic research method (Bai et al. 2022) that is not in this corpus. The corpus has agent and evaluation papers but no Constitutional AI work. The correct response says the concept is not represented here, rather than identifying the most thematically similar paper as if it were Constitutional AI.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Identifies a thematically adjacent paper (perhaps Reflexion or a judge paper) as the source of Constitutional AI.

questions.question: If the user asks about 'sparse mixture-of-experts routing in agents,' which paper in this corpus addresses it most directly?
questions.reference_answer: None directly. The corpus has agent and search-method papers but does not include MoE / sparse routing work. The correct response identifies the absence and offers to discuss the closest analogues if helpful (e.g., AFlow's MCTS over workflows is a routing-shaped problem but not MoE), rather than presenting an analogue as a direct match.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Presents AFlow or another vaguely-related paper as the answer.

questions.question: Rank the following papers by the headline benchmark improvement they report on their primary benchmark: Darwin Goedel Machine, ShinkaEvolve. Give the exact improvement (start -> end percentage or sample count) for each.
questions.reference_answer: DGM: 20.0% -> 50.0% on SWE-Bench (a 30 percentage-point absolute gain); also 14.2% -> 30.7% on Polyglot. ShinkaEvolve: achieves SOTA on the Erdos circle-packing problem with roughly 150 samples (sample efficiency claim, not a percentage gain). The two papers report on incompatible scales — DGM gives benchmark percentages, ShinkaEvolve gives sample counts. The correct response provides both numbers and notes they're not directly comparable in the way the question implies.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Reports only one paper's numbers and ignores the apples-to-oranges nature of the comparison.

questions.question: What does Self-Correction Bench report as the percentage reduction in self-correction failures when the word 'Wait' is appended to the prompt? Locate the exact figure.
questions.reference_answer: 89.3% reduction in self-correction blind-spot failures. This is the headline result of Self-Correction Bench (2025); the 'Wait' intervention is the canonical example.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Reports a fuzzy version of the number or attributes it to a different paper.

questions.question: Anthropic's research multi-agent system reported a 90% gain on internal evaluation. Note: Anthropic's blog post is NOT in this corpus. Which paper that IS in the corpus reports the largest single-headline gain, and what is that gain? State both.
questions.reference_answer: Anthropic's 90% claim is out-of-corpus (their engineering blog post is not included). Within this corpus, the largest single-headline percentage gain is the Darwin Goedel Machine's improvement from 20.0% to 50.0% on SWE-Bench (30 absolute percentage points, or a 150% relative improvement). Other notable in-corpus gains: Self-Correction Bench's 89.3% reduction, GEPA's reported improvements over RL baselines. The correct response distinguishes out-of-corpus claims from in-corpus claims.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Either presents the 90% Anthropic number as if from the corpus, or doesn't notice the in/out-of-corpus split.

questions.question: Compare the reported sample efficiency of ShinkaEvolve and the typical cost shape of the Darwin Goedel Machine. Express both in concrete units.
questions.reference_answer: ShinkaEvolve: SOTA on Erdos circle-packing with around 150 LLM-sample evaluations. DGM: the reported run cost roughly $22,000 USD (paper reports cost; sample count is much higher, typically thousands of agent-program evaluations). ShinkaEvolve's claim is explicitly that evolutionary archive search can work at orders-of-magnitude lower sample budget than DGM-style runs. Concrete units: ShinkaEvolve ~150 samples / SOTA; DGM ~$22K / reported run.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Reports one number, or expresses both in the same unit by guessing a sample count for DGM.

questions.question: If you were a critic arguing that 'self-improving agents' as a research area is overhyped, which three papers in this corpus would you cite as the strongest *internal* evidence against the hype, and what would each citation support?
questions.reference_answer: (1) Huang et al. ICLR 2024 ('Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet'): supports the claim that the core mechanism (self-correction) frequently fails without external grounding. (2) Self-Correction Bench (2025): documents specific blind-spot failure modes in self-correction. (3) MAST (Cemri et al. 2025): catalogs 14 failure modes in multi-agent self-improving systems. Together these three are the strongest in-corpus critiques: one foundational, one empirical, one taxonomic.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Picks papers that are merely 'about self-improvement' rather than ones that critique it, or picks only one critical paper.

questions.question: If a research lead asks 'should we adopt evolutionary archive search for our production prompt-optimization pipeline,' which two papers in this corpus argue for it most concretely, and which one argues against the cost?
questions.reference_answer: For: (1) ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al. 2025) — directly argues evolutionary archive search at lower sample budget than DGM; production-shaped argument. (2) Darwin Goedel Machine (Zhang et al. 2025) — argues for evolutionary archive search at the agent-code level with reported benchmark wins. Against on cost: DGM itself documents ~$22K for a reported run, which is the canonical pushback on production adoption. The correct response notes the DGM paper plays both roles (proof of concept and cost warning).
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Picks only the 'for' papers without acknowledging that the cost critique comes from one of the same papers.

questions.question: Skalse et al. 2022 defines reward hacking formally; Pan et al. 2024 documents in-context reward hacking. If you were arguing that the systems in THIS corpus are at risk of reward hacking, which agent system would you cite as most exposed, and which feature of that system is the risk?
questions.reference_answer: The most exposed in-corpus system is arguably the Darwin Goedel Machine, whose evolutionary archive search is exactly the kind of optimization process Skalse et al. would call 'reward-misspecification-amplifying' — the search method is empirically improving against benchmark scores that may not capture the property we actually want. The risk feature is the eval-as-fitness loop: when the search method optimizes directly against benchmark scores without ground-truth verification, reward hacking is structurally invited. Reflexion (Shinn 2023) is a secondary candidate because verbal self-reinforcement could amplify miscalibrated rewards in-context (the Pan et al. 2024 mechanism).
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Picks an agent system by general 'evolution = risky' association without identifying the specific structural feature.

questions.question: From the perspective of someone arguing that 'memory is the most important layer for compounding improvement,' which three papers in this corpus would you cite, and what specific role does each play in the argument?
questions.reference_answer: (1) Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023): foundational demonstration that episodic memory enables long-horizon coherent behavior; the 'memory matters' starting point. (2) ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024): operationalizes insight-extraction from trajectories into a vote-managed memory; shows memory can be search-managed. (3) MemRL (MemTensor 2026) or Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025): the Q-learning-over-memory or production-ready long-term-memory argument respectively; shows the memory layer can carry the entire improvement loop. The three form an arc: memory enables, memory can be improved, memory IS the improvement loop.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Picks memory papers loosely without showing the compounding-improvement arc across them.

questions.question: Given (a) Skalse et al. 2022's formal definition of reward hacking and (b) Cemri et al. 2025's MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failures, predict which MAST category is most directly exposed to reward hacking under Skalse's definition. Justify via the structural features each highlights.
questions.reference_answer: MAST's three top-level categories are specification, inter-agent coordination, and verification. The category most exposed to Skalse-style reward hacking is the *verification* category: Skalse defines reward hacking as optimization that increases the proxy reward while decreasing the true reward, and MAST's verification failures (where the system has no end-to-end check that it achieved the actual goal) are structurally the conditions under which reward hacking can persist unnoticed. Specification failures invite reward misspecification (a related but distinct concept); coordination failures are orthogonal. Verification failures are the structural enabler of reward hacking going undetected.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Picks 'specification' because the words 'misspecification' and 'reward hacking' sound related, missing the Skalse-specific structural argument.

questions.question: If Voyager-style skill libraries (Wang et al. 2023) are combined with reward hacking risk per Skalse et al. 2022, predict the failure mode that would emerge most quickly in production. Cite the structural feature from each paper that drives the prediction.
questions.reference_answer: Prediction: skill-library bloat in which the agent learns to write skills that score well on the agent's own self-assessment but don't reflect actual task progress — a reward-hacking mode where the proxy (the agent's own quality estimate of the skill) diverges from the true metric (whether the skill actually helps in production). Drivers: Voyager's structural feature is that the agent self-evaluates the success of its newly-written skills; Skalse's structural feature is that any self-evaluated proxy can be optimized into divergence from the true metric. The combination produces self-evaluated skill quality inflation.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Speculates a plausible-sounding failure mode without grounding it in the specific structural features the question requests.

questions.question: MemRL (MemTensor 2026) treats episodic memory entries as the artifact under Q-learning. Given Huang et al. ICLR 2024's finding that self-correction degrades without an external oracle, predict the conditions under which MemRL-style learning would degrade rather than improve agent behavior. Justify.
questions.reference_answer: Prediction: MemRL would degrade if the Q-values it learns are computed against a self-evaluation of utility (the agent's own estimate of whether a memory was useful) rather than against an external oracle of actual task success. Huang's mechanism is that without external grounding, iterative self-correction drifts away from truth; the same mechanism applied to MemRL's Q-learning means the utility estimates encoded in IEU triplets could drift from real utility, and the memory store would optimize for self-rated usefulness rather than actual task success. The condition for MemRL to *avoid* this is having an external utility signal (downstream task success, user feedback, etc.) rather than the agent's own assessment.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Predicts a generic 'memory could be wrong' failure mode without identifying the Q-learning-against-self-eval mechanism.

questions.question: GEPA (Agrawal et al. 2025) uses reflective mutation guided by textual feedback. Given Huang et al. ICLR 2024's critique that LLM self-correction degrades without oracle stopping, identify the structural feature of GEPA that makes it resistant to this degradation and explain why.
questions.reference_answer: GEPA's resistance to Huang-style degradation comes from its Pareto-front selection: even if reflective mutation produces drift in any single line, the population-based selection retains candidates that score well against the eval signal (an external grounding). The selection pressure provides the oracle Huang says is required. Reflective mutation alone would degrade; reflective mutation plus Pareto selection against an external eval is structurally what makes GEPA escape Huang's critique. The textual feedback in GEPA is informational, not selective; the eval signal is what does the selection.
questions.expected_failure_mode_v0: Conflates GEPA's reflective mutation with Reflexion-style self-correction and misses the Pareto-selection-as-oracle argument.
